h1: How Much Protein Per Day? Daily Protein Intake Calculator
description: How much protein do you need per day? Enter your weight and goal to get your grams/day. Active adults: 0.5–0.7 g/lb; muscle gain: 0.7–1.0 g/lb; cutting: ~0.8–1.1 g/lb. Free table included.
answerSnippet: Most active adults need 0.5–0.7 g of protein per pound of body weight per day (1.2–1.6 g/kg). For muscle gain aim for 0.7–1.0 g/lb (1.6–2.2 g/kg); when cutting in a calorie deficit, 0.8–1.1 g/lb (1.8–2.4 g/kg). A 180 lb (82 kg) active adult needs about 98–131 g/day — roughly 3–4 chicken breasts or 14–19 large eggs. Multiply your weight in lb by the g/lb factor for your goal.
intro: Protein is the most leverage-heavy macro for body composition, recovery, and aging well — and the right dose depends entirely on your goal. The US RDA of **0.36 g/lb** (0.8 g/kg) is a sedentary floor designed to prevent nitrogen-balance deficiency, not a target for anyone who trains hard. The ISSN 2017 Position Stand puts active adults at **0.5–0.7 g/lb** (1.2–1.6 g/kg), muscle gain phases at **0.7–1.0 g/lb** (1.6–2.2 g/kg), and cutting at roughly **0.8–1.1 g/lb** (1.8–2.4 g/kg) to preserve lean body mass in a calorie deficit. Adults 65+ need a higher target — this calculator adds a **+20% senior adjustment** automatically — to counter sarcopenia and anabolic resistance (Phillips 2015, Am J Clin Nutr; ESPEN 2019). Per-meal distribution matters as much as the daily total: muscle protein synthesis (MPS) plateaus at roughly **0.4 g/lb per meal**, and each feeding should hit the **2.5–3 g leucine threshold** to trigger a full MPS pulse (Schoenfeld & Aragon 2018). This calculator gives you both the daily total and a per-meal target, with food equivalents in standard US servings (oz, large eggs, scoops of whey).
keyTakeaway: A 180 lb (82 kg) active adult needs roughly 98–131 g of protein per day — equivalent to about 3–4 chicken breasts or 14–19 large eggs.
useCases: Setting a daily protein target for a lean bulk (0.7–1.0 g/lb) to maximize muscle gain without excess fat
Cutting phase LBM preservation — hitting 1.0–1.2 g/lb in a 500 kcal deficit while strength training
Vegan athlete protein optimization — combining sources (soy, pea, rice + lentils) to hit DIAAS-equivalent intake
Sarcopenia prevention for adults 60+ — 0.5–0.7 g/lb spread across 3–4 meals with 2.5–3 g leucine each
Pre-sleep casein dosing for overnight MPS (30–40 g slow-digesting protein)

Reverse-dieting after a long cut — anchoring protein at 1.0 g/lb while carbs and fats ramp

options.label: Cut (Lose Fat) — lifting in a calorie deficit

explanation:
## What Is Daily Protein Intake (in g/lb terms)

Daily protein intake is the total grams of protein you consume across a 24-hour window to support muscle protein synthesis (MPS), recovery, immune function, and lean mass preservation. In the US, the RDA is **0.36 g per pound** of body weight (0.8 g/kg) — but that figure was calibrated on sedentary adults and represents the minimum to prevent nitrogen-balance deficiency. For anyone who lifts, runs, or actively manages body composition, the evidence-based target is meaningfully higher.

## Goal-Based Targets (g/lb Primary)

| Goal | Range (g/lb) | Range (g/kg) | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sedentary RDA | 0.36 | 0.8 | DRI 2005 (floor) |
| Active / general fitness | 0.5–0.7 | 1.2–1.6 | ISSN 2017 |
| Muscle gain (bulk) | 0.7–1.0 | 1.6–2.2 | Morton 2018 meta |
| Cutting (deficit + lifting) | 0.8–1.1 | 1.8–2.4 | Helms 2014; ISSN 2017 |
| Elderly (65+ sarcopenia) | 0.6–0.8 | 1.4–1.8 | Phillips 2015; ESPEN (+20%) |

The calculator applies these exact g/kg ranges, converts your weight to kilograms, and adds a +20% adjustment automatically if you enter an age of 65 or older (ESPEN 2019 senior guidance for anabolic resistance).

## How Much Protein Per Day by Body Weight (Active, 1.2–1.6 g/kg)

This is the quick reference for the most common goal — active adults. Multiply your weight by the g/lb factor for any other goal.

| Body weight | Active (g/day) | Muscle gain (g/day) | Cutting (g/day) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 120 lb (54 kg) | 65–87 | 87–120 | 98–131 |
| 140 lb (64 kg) | 76–102 | 102–140 | 114–152 |
| 150 lb (68 kg) | 82–109 | 109–150 | 122–163 |
| 160 lb (73 kg) | 87–116 | 116–160 | 131–174 |
| 170 lb (77 kg) | 93–123 | 123–170 | 139–185 |
| 180 lb (82 kg) | 98–131 | 131–180 | 147–196 |
| 190 lb (86 kg) | 103–138 | 138–190 | 155–207 |
| 200 lb (91 kg) | 109–145 | 145–200 | 163–218 |
| 220 lb (100 kg) | 120–160 | 160–220 | 180–239 |

**The exact factors:** convert lb→kg by dividing by 2.2046, then multiply by your goal's g/kg range — active 1.2–1.6, muscle gain 1.6–2.2, cutting 1.8–2.4, sedentary RDA 0.8. In g/lb terms that is roughly: active 0.54–0.73, muscle gain 0.73–1.0, cutting 0.82–1.09, sedentary 0.36.

## Worked Examples

**Cutting — 180 lb (82 kg) lifter at 1.8–2.4 g/kg:**
82 × 1.8 = 147 g and 82 × 2.4 = 196 g → **147–196 g protein/day**, ideally split across 4 meals of ~40–50 g each.

**Bulking — 180 lb (82 kg) lifter at 1.6–2.2 g/kg:**
82 × 1.6 = 131 g and 82 × 2.2 = 180 g → **131–180 g protein/day**, with one feeding being a 30–40 g pre-sleep casein dose.

**Female lifter — 140 lb (63.5 kg) cutting at 1.8–2.4 g/kg:**
63.5 × 1.8 = 114 g and 63.5 × 2.4 = 152 g → **114–152 g/day**, split ~35 g × 4 meals to stay above the leucine threshold each feeding.

## Per-Meal Limit: The 0.4 g/lb MPS Plateau

Muscle protein synthesis is not unlimited per bolus. Schoenfeld and Aragon (2018, J Int Soc Sports Nutr) showed MPS plateaus at roughly **0.4 g/lb per meal** (0.55 g/kg) in trained lifters — meaning a 180 lb athlete maxes out MPS at about 72 g per sitting, with anything above that oxidized for energy or converted to urea. The practical takeaway: spreading protein across **4 evenly-spaced meals** beats a single large feeding (Areta et al. 2013 — same daily total, but the 4×20g protocol produced higher 12-hour MPS than 2×40g or 8×10g).

## Leucine Threshold: 2.5–3 g Per Meal

Leucine is the branched-chain amino acid that flips the mTOR switch and initiates MPS. Each feeding needs **2.5–3 g of leucine** to trigger a full anabolic response. This translates to roughly 25–30 g of high-quality animal protein (whey, eggs, chicken, lean beef) or 40–50 g of most plant proteins. Skipping the threshold at a meal effectively wastes that anabolic window.

## Protein Source Comparison (per 100 g)

| Source | Protein (g) | DIAAS | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Whey isolate | 90 | 1.09 | Fastest absorption, MPS spike |
| Chicken breast (cooked) | 31 | — | US gym-bro default |
| Lean beef (sirloin) | 26 | — | Plus creatine, B12, iron |
| Salmon | 25 | — | Omega-3 bonus |
| Tempeh | 19 | 0.94 | Best non-soy plant source |
| Tofu (firm) | 15 | 0.99 | Soy = highest DIAAS plant protein |
| Eggs (whole) | 13 | 1.13 | Whites only: 11 g |
| Greek yogurt (full-fat) | 10 | 1.18 | Best DIAAS of any food |
| Cottage cheese | 11 | — | Slow casein, pre-sleep option |
| Lentils (cooked) | 9 | 0.65 | Combine with rice for complete AA |

**DIAAS rankings** (Digestible Indispensable Amino Acid Score) — milk 1.18 > eggs 1.13 > whey 1.09 > tofu 0.99 > pea 0.93 > lentils 0.65 > wheat 0.40. Anything above 1.0 is considered complete; wheat's score reflects its lysine deficiency.

## Pre-Sleep Casein: 30–40 g

Snijders et al. (2015) demonstrated that 40 g of casein consumed 30 min before sleep elevated overnight MPS by 22% versus placebo, with no negative effect on morning hunger or appetite. Casein's slow digestion provides a 6–8 hour amino acid drip — ideal for the overnight fast. Cottage cheese (28 g protein per cup) is a whole-food alternative.

## Vegan Protein Quality

Plant proteins typically score lower on DIAAS due to one or more limiting amino acids. The fix is combination: **rice + lentils**, **beans + corn tortillas**, or **soy + grains** all yield complete amino acid profiles. Vegan athletes should target the **upper end of each range** (0.7 g/lb active, 1.0 g/lb bulking) to compensate for lower digestibility. Soy isolate, pea protein, and tempeh are the highest-quality vegan options.

## Female vs. Male Targets

The g/lb ratio is identical between sexes — what changes is the absolute gram total because body weight differs. A 140 lb female lifter cutting at 1.0 g/lb needs 140 g/day; a 180 lb male at the same g/lb needs 180 g. Some research suggests women may be slightly more efficient at MPS during the luteal phase, but practical targets remain weight-based.

## Elderly Anabolic Resistance (+10–20% per meal)

Adults 60+ require more protein per meal to overcome anabolic resistance — the reduced MPS response to a given protein dose (Phillips 2015, Am J Clin Nutr). Where a young lifter maxes MPS at 0.4 g/lb per meal, a senior needs roughly 0.45–0.5 g/lb per meal to hit the same anabolic ceiling. This is why the ISSN and ESPEN both recommend seniors target the upper bound of their range, distributed across 3–4 meals.

## Does High Protein Damage Healthy Kidneys?

No — this is one of the most-cited myths in sports nutrition. Devries et al. (2018, J Nutr meta-analysis) reviewed 28 studies and found **no adverse effect** of high-protein diets (>1.5 g/kg) on glomerular filtration rate in healthy adults. Antonio et al. (2016) followed lifters consuming **3.0 g/kg** for a year with no markers of kidney dysfunction. The kidney-damage concern applies only to individuals with pre-existing chronic kidney disease (CKD), who should not exceed 0.36 g/lb without medical supervision.

## Limitations

- **Body composition not factored.** Lean-mass calculations (using BF%) may yield lower targets for higher-BF individuals.
- **CKD contraindication.** Do not exceed 0.36 g/lb if you have chronic kidney disease.
- **Pregnancy/lactation.** Needs increase 25–50 g/day; this calculator does not cover those scenarios.
- **Ranges, not absolutes.** Individual response varies; use this as a starting point for a 4–8 week trial.

faq.q: What's the right protein g/lb for cutting vs. bulking?
faq.a: Cutting (lifting in a calorie deficit) requires more protein than bulking — counterintuitive, but true. Helms et al. (2014) and the ISSN 2017 Position Stand recommend roughly 1.8–2.4 g/kg (about 0.8–1.1 g/lb) when cutting to preserve lean body mass, versus 1.6–2.2 g/kg (0.7–1.0 g/lb) for muscle gain. The logic: in a deficit, the body has less energy available and is more likely to break down muscle for fuel, so higher protein creates a defensive buffer. A 180 lb (82 kg) lifter cutting hits ~147–196 g/day; bulking hits ~131–180 g/day.

faq.q: Can the body really only absorb 30 g of protein per meal?
faq.a: No — this is one of the most stubborn gym myths. The body absorbs essentially all protein you eat; what's actually limited is muscle protein synthesis (MPS), which plateaus at roughly 0.4 g/lb per meal (Schoenfeld & Aragon 2018). For a 180 lb lifter that's about 72 g per sitting before MPS maxes out. Protein above that ceiling isn't 'wasted' — it's oxidized for energy or used for other amino acid pools. The practical implication is that spreading protein across 4 meals beats one giant 200 g feeding, not that single meals over 30 g are pointless.

faq.q: What's the best protein source for muscle gain?
faq.a: By DIAAS score, the top-tier sources are milk (1.18), eggs (1.13), and whey (1.09) — all complete proteins with excellent leucine content. For whole-food eating, chicken breast (31 g per 100 g), lean beef (26 g), and salmon (25 g) are the gym-standard staples in the US. Whey isolate is the most cost-effective post-workout option due to its fast absorption and leucine concentration. For convenience, Greek yogurt and cottage cheese deliver complete protein with slow-digesting casein for overnight MPS.

faq.q: Whey vs. casein — what's the actual difference?
faq.a: Whey is fast-absorbing (peak amino acid levels in 60–90 min) and spikes MPS quickly — ideal post-workout. Casein is slow-absorbing (sustained amino acid release over 6–8 hours) and ideal pre-sleep. Snijders et al. (2015) showed 40 g of casein 30 min before bed boosted overnight MPS 22% versus placebo with no morning appetite drag. Most lifters benefit from whey post-training and casein (or cottage cheese) pre-bed. For everyone else, either works — total daily protein matters more than the specific isolate.

faq.q: Does high protein damage your kidneys?
faq.a: Not in healthy adults. Devries et al. (2018, J Nutr) meta-analyzed 28 studies on protein and kidney function and found no adverse effect of high-protein diets (above 1.5 g/kg) on glomerular filtration rate or kidney markers in healthy adults. Antonio et al. (2016) followed trained lifters consuming 3.0 g/kg daily for a year with no kidney dysfunction. The kidney concern is real — but only for people with pre-existing chronic kidney disease (CKD), who should stay at 0.36 g/lb (RDA) or below under medical supervision.

faq.q: Can vegans get enough protein on plant sources alone?
faq.a: Yes, but with two adjustments: target the upper bound of each range (0.7 g/lb active, 1.0 g/lb bulking) to compensate for lower DIAAS scores, and combine complementary proteins to cover all essential amino acids. Best combinations: rice + lentils, beans + corn tortillas, soy + grains. Soy (tofu, tempeh, edamame) and pea protein isolate are the highest-quality vegan sources — both score above 0.9 on DIAAS. Vegan lifters consistently hit 1.0 g/lb without issues using soy isolate, lentils, tempeh, seitan, and a daily B12 supplement.

faq.q: Is pre-bed protein actually worth it?
faq.a: Yes for serious lifters, optional for general fitness. Snijders et al. (2015) showed 40 g of casein 30 min before sleep elevated overnight muscle protein synthesis by 22% versus placebo, with no negative effects on morning appetite or sleep quality. The mechanism: casein's slow digestion provides a 6–8 hour amino acid drip during the overnight fast, when MPS would otherwise drop. For someone training 4+ days/week trying to maximize lean mass, this is meaningful. Cottage cheese (28 g/cup) is a whole-food equivalent.

faq.q: How much leucine do I need per meal?
faq.a: 2.5–3 g of leucine per meal triggers a full muscle protein synthesis pulse — this is called the leucine threshold. Hitting it requires roughly 25–30 g of high-quality animal protein (whey, eggs, lean meat) or 40–50 g of most plant proteins. Whey isolate has the highest leucine concentration (~12% by weight); soy protein is the highest plant source. The implication: a meal with only 15 g of plant protein may not cross the threshold even if it has 'enough' total protein.

faq.q: Do older adults really need more protein?
faq.a: Yes — and per meal, not just per day. Older adults experience anabolic resistance: muscles respond less efficiently to a given protein dose due to reduced mTOR signaling. Phillips et al. (2015, Am J Clin Nutr) recommends 1.2–1.5 g/kg (about 0.5–0.7 g/lb) daily for healthy seniors, with each meal hitting roughly 0.45–0.5 g/lb to overcome the resistance. This calculator automatically adds a +20% adjustment when you enter an age of 65 or older (ESPEN 2019). In practice that means 30–40 g of high-quality protein per meal × 3–4 meals/day. Combined with resistance training, this is the most-studied strategy to prevent sarcopenia (age-related muscle loss).

faq.q: Does protein timing matter or just total daily intake?
faq.a: Both matter, but daily total dominates. Schoenfeld's meta-analyses show that hitting your daily target (0.7–1.2 g/lb depending on goal) is roughly 80% of the benefit, with distribution providing the remaining edge. The optimal protocol per Areta et al. (2013, J Physiol): 4 evenly-spaced meals of 0.3–0.4 g/lb each. This beat both 2 large meals and 8 small meals at the same total. The post-workout 'anabolic window' is wider than once thought — Schoenfeld 2013 showed it extends 4–6 hours, not 30 minutes.

faq.q: How much protein is in common US foods?
faq.a: Per USDA FoodData Central: 4 oz cooked chicken breast = 35 g; 4 oz lean ground beef (90/10) = 27 g; 4 oz salmon = 25 g; 1 large egg = 6.3 g; 1 cup Greek yogurt (plain, full-fat) = 17–20 g; 1 cup cottage cheese = 28 g; 1 scoop whey isolate (30 g) = 25 g; 1/2 cup firm tofu = 20 g; 3 oz canned tuna = 22 g; 1 cup cooked lentils = 18 g. These are reference values — actual brands vary, so check labels for precision tracking.
